title: The AI generation gap: Are Gen Z students more interested in adopting generative AI such as ChatGPT in teaching and learning than their Gen X and millennial generation teachers?
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether there is a generational gap in higher education regarding the adoption of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The study asks how Gen Z students compare with Gen X and Gen Y teachers in their experiences, perceptions, knowledge, concerns, and intentions around using generative AI in teaching and learning. The motivating problem is that higher education institutions are facing rapid uptake of GenAI tools without established policies, while students and teachers may differ in readiness, expectations, and concerns.

The authors used a mixed-methods online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and with t-tests comparing students and teachers, while qualitative responses were coded thematically. The survey focused on current use of GenAI, beliefs about its benefits and risks, and intended uses in academic work. This was not an intervention study; rather, it investigated naturally occurring attitudes and self-reported behaviors related to generative AI adoption.

The sample included 583 participants: 399 students and 184 teachers, primarily from higher education contexts associated with Hong Kong, with additional participants from Mainland China, the UK/Ireland, Australia, North America, and East Asia. The student population included undergraduate, taught postgraduate, and research postgraduate students, while the teacher group included professors, lecturers, postdoctoral staff, and teaching/research assistants. The context was higher education, and data were collected through an online survey in early 2023.

The study found that students were generally more optimistic and reported more frequent use of GenAI than teachers. Students were more likely to see benefits such as time savings, writing support, and positive long-term impacts on teaching and learning. Teachers also recognized potential benefits but expressed stronger concerns about factual inaccuracies, bias, overreliance, academic integrity, and weakened student skill development. Both groups emphasized the need for institutional guidelines, AI literacy, critical thinking, and responsible integration rather than outright bans. The paper concludes that effective higher education use of GenAI should combine technological opportunities with human teaching, policy development, and support for responsible use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models that generates conversational text, answers questions, and assists with writing and information synthesis.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an example of generative AI in higher education; surveyed students and teachers reported their experiences, perceptions, concerns, and intended uses of ChatGPT for writing, information gathering, feedback, brainstorming, language learning, and teaching support.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-method survey, students reported more frequent use of generative AI technologies like ChatGPT than teachers (students: M=2.27, SD=1.65; teachers: M=2.03, SD=1.11; t(581)=2.28, p=.023). Students also agreed more strongly that ChatGPT could help save time (students: M=4.16, SD=0.83; teachers: M=3.90, SD=0.88; t(555)=3.38, p<.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of GenAI use and perceived time-saving benefit

findings.finding_summary: Students were more likely than teachers to believe that integrating ChatGPT/GenAI into higher education would positively affect teaching and learning in the long run (students: M=3.90, SD=0.82; teachers: M=3.58, SD=1.11; t(234)=3.36, p<.001). Qualitative responses from both groups described intended uses for brainstorming, summarizing, writing support, feedback, and personalized learning, but teachers also raised concerns that use could undermine learning in areas such as writing and language development.
findings.measure: Perceived long-run impact on teaching and learning; qualitative intended educational uses

findings.finding_summary: Students showed higher agreement than teachers that ChatGPT could help students become better writers (students: M=3.29, SD=1.16; teachers: M=3.06, SD=1.23; t(545)=2.07, p=.039). Qualitative data indicated both students and teachers intended to use ChatGPT for essay structure, organization, grammar checks, proofreading, and improving arguments, while some participants argued it could hinder authentic writing and creativity.
findings.measure: Perceived writing improvement and qualitative writing-support uses

findings.finding_summary: Students were more likely than teachers to view ChatGPT/AI as a useful tool for student support services because of anonymity (students: M=3.73, SD=1.01; teachers: M=3.53, SD=1.11; t(536)=2.07, p=.039). However, teachers were more concerned that GenAI would limit students' opportunities to interact with others and socialize when completing coursework (students: M=3.09, SD=1.19; teachers: M=3.43, SD=1.14; t(542)=-3.16, p=.002).
findings.measure: Perceived usefulness for anonymous student support and perceived effect on social interaction

findings.finding_summary: Teachers expressed substantially greater concern than students that students could become over-reliant on ChatGPT/GenAI (students: M=2.87, SD=1.14; teachers: M=4.12, SD=0.89; t(425)=-14.00, p<.001). Qualitative responses linked this concern to reduced critical thinking, weaker evaluative ability, and possible hampering of essential skill development.
findings.measure: Perceived over-reliance on GenAI and qualitative concerns about critical-thinking/skill development

findings.finding_summary: Both groups generally agreed that higher education institutions should have a plan in place for managing risks associated with ChatGPT/GenAI (students: M=4.47, SD=0.83; teachers: M=4.53, SD=0.86; t(573)=-0.79, p=.432) and that students must learn to use GenAI well for their careers (students: M=3.97, SD=0.98; teachers: M=3.96, SD=0.98; t(556)=0.02, p=.987). Qualitative findings emphasized urgent need for policies, guidelines, assessment redesign, digital literacy, and responsible-use protocols rather than bans.
findings.measure: Agreement on institutional planning and career-related need to learn GenAI use; qualitative policy implications

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-method survey study with descriptive statistics, t-tests, and qualitative thematic analysis, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of learning outcomes caused by the tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports attitudes, intentions, and concerns rather than causal effect sizes on student learning; impacts are mixed and largely perception-based, so overall impact is unclear.
